label: Linear Equations in Two Variables
overview: Two linear equations in two unknowns form a system whose solution is the point where both lines intersect. SAT questions ask you to solve the system, determine how many solutions exist, or identify what change to one equation would create no solution or infinite solutions. Substitution and elimination are the two algebraic methods.

keyFormulas.name: Substitution method
keyFormulas.latex: \text{Solve one equation for one variable, substitute into the other}

keyFormulas.name: Elimination method
keyFormulas.latex: \text{Multiply equations so one variable cancels when added}

keyFormulas.name: Infinite solutions
keyFormulas.latex: \text{Equations are multiples of each other (same line)}

workedExamples.problem: Solve the system: 2x + y = 7 and x − y = 2.

steps.title: Use elimination — add the equations
steps.content: The y terms are opposites (+y and −y), so adding eliminates y immediately.

steps.title: Substitute back to find y
steps.content: Plug x = 3 into the simpler equation.

commonMistakes.mistake: Multiplying only some terms when scaling an equation for elimination
commonMistakes.fix: Multiply every term on both sides by the scalar — treat the entire equation.
Always substitute back to find the second variable. The answer is a coordinate pair (x, y).

quickTip: If the system looks easy to eliminate (coefficients are already equal or opposite), use elimination. If one equation already has x = or y =, use substitution.
